content: Radiation therapy involves the therapeutic application of ionizing radiation and high-energy elementary particle beams in the treatment of patients. Radiology focuses on the interpretation of various imaging modalities, including X-rays, ultrasound, radioisotopes, and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). A more recent branch of radiology, known as interventional radiology, utilizes medical devices to access specific areas of the body using minimally invasive techniques. Surgical specialties are centered on operative treatments. These include fields such as orthopedics, urology, ophthalmology, neurosurgery, plastic surgery, otolaryngology, and subspecialties like transplant surgery and cardiothoracic surgery. Some disciplines, while highly specialized, are not always considered subdivisions of surgery despite their names suggesting otherwise. Urgent care is dedicated to providing unscheduled, walk-in medical attention outside of hospital emergency departments for injuries and illnesses that do not require the level of care provided in an emergency department. Interdisciplinary Fields Interdisciplinary sub-specialties in medicine include: Aerospace medicine, which addresses medical issues related to flying and space travel. Bioethics, a field that examines the intersection of biology, science, medicine, ethics, philosophy, and theology. Biomedical engineering, which applies engineering principles to medical practice. Clinical pharmacology, which studies the interaction of therapeutic systems with patients. Conservation medicine, which explores the relationship between human and animal health and environmental conditions. This field is also referred to as ecological medicine, environmental medicine, or medical geology. Disaster medicine, which focuses on the medical aspects of emergency preparedness, disaster mitigation, and management. Diving medicine (or hyperbaric medicine), which involves the prevention and treatment of medical conditions related to diving. Evolutionary medicine, which applies evolutionary theory to medical practice. Forensic medicine, which deals with medical questions in legal contexts, such as determining the time and cause of death. Keraunomedicine, the study of medical issues related to lightning injuries. Medical humanities, which integrates humanities (literature, philosophy, ethics, history, and religion), social sciences (anthropology, cultural studies, psychology, sociology), and the arts (literature, theater, film, and visual arts) into medical education and practice. Medical informatics, a relatively new field that applies computer science and information technology to medicine, including eHealth. Naturopathic medicine, which emphasizes primary care, natural remedies, patient education, and disease prevention. Nosology, the classification of diseases for various purposes. Occupational medicine, which addresses medical issues related to work and the working environment. Osteopathic medicine, which posits that many diseases result from problems with bones and joints. Pharmacogenomics, a form of personalized medicine. Sports medicine, which focuses on the treatment and prevention of injuries in athletes, both amateur and professional. The sports medicine team typically includes specialty physicians, surgeons, athletic trainers, physical therapists, coaches, and the athletes themselves. Therapeutics, an older term referring to the study of remedies used to treat diseases and promote health. Travel medicine (or emporiatrics), which deals with health issues faced by international travelers or those moving across diverse environments. Medical Education Medical education encompasses the training required to become a medical practitioner, including both initial training and further specialization. The structure of medical education varies globally but typically involves entry-level education at a university medical school, followed by supervised practice (internship and/or residency) and potentially postgraduate vocational training. Continuing medical education is mandated by many regulatory authorities. Various teaching methodologies are employed in medical education, which remains an active area of educational research. In England, a standard medical course at a university lasts five years (or four years for students with a prior degree). For some institutions and students, it may extend to six years if an intercalated BSc is chosen, adding an additional year after pre-clinical studies. This is followed by two Foundation years (F1 and F2). Students register with the UK General Medical Council at the end of F1 and may pursue further study after F2. In Australia, students have two pathways: a six-year undergraduate Bachelor of Medicine/Bachelor of Surgery (MBBS) program directly from high school, or an undergraduate degree followed by a four-year Bachelor of Medicine/Bachelor of Surgery (BMBS) program. Legal Restrictions In most countries, medical doctors are legally required to be licensed or registered. This typically involves obtaining a medical degree from a university and accreditation by a medical board or equivalent national organization, which may require passing examinations. These regulations ensure that the significant legal authority of the medical profession is restricted to physicians trained and qualified according to national standards. They also serve as a safeguard for patients and a deterrent against unqualified individuals practicing inadequate medicine for personal gain. While these laws generally require medical doctors to be trained in evidence-based, Western, or Hippocratic medicine, they are not intended to discourage alternative paradigms of health. Criticism Criticism of medicine has a long history. During the Middle Ages, some viewed medicine as unsuitable for Christians, as disease was often considered a divine punishment or test. God was seen as the divine physician who sent illness or healing according to His will. However, many monastic orders, particularly the Benedictines, regarded caring for the sick as a primary act of mercy. Barber-surgeons historically had a poor reputation, which only improved with the development of academic surgery as a recognized medical specialty rather than an auxiliary field. In the 20th century, healthcare providers increasingly focused on technological advancements that significantly improved patient outcomes. However, this shift toward a more mechanistic and detached practice, often referred to as the medical model of health, led to criticism for its perceived loss of patient-centered care.
